passages.t: Pharaoh's dreams, and a cupbearer remembers
passages.happening:
“After two full years had passed, Pharaoh had a dream: He was standing beside the Nile” (verse 1). Seven fat cows come up out of the river. Seven thin cows come up after them and eat the fat ones (verses 2-4).

He sleeps again and dreams a second time. Seven full heads of grain grow on one stalk. Seven thin ones, “scorched by the east wind” (verse 6), swallow them up (verses 5-7).

In the morning Pharaoh is troubled. He calls all the magicians and wise men of Egypt, “but no one could interpret them for him” (verse 8).

Then the chief cupbearer speaks. “Today I recall my failures” (verse 9). He tells Pharaoh about the young Hebrew in prison who explained his dream and the baker's, “And it happened to us just as he had interpreted” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Two full years. That is how long Joseph waited after the cupbearer forgot him. Joseph was seventeen when his brothers sold him (37:2). He will be thirty when he stands before Pharaoh (verse 46). Thirteen years lie between his boyhood dreams and the first sign that they will come true.

Pharaoh was the title of Egypt's king. Genesis never tells us which Pharaoh this was.

The Nile was Egypt's life. Every year the river flooded and watered the fields. If the flood was too low, the harvest failed. So a dream of cows coming up out of the Nile, fat and then thin, would chill an Egyptian. Cattle grazed on the green reeds by the river. The east wind was the hot, dry wind from the desert that scorched the crops.

The magicians and wise men were Egypt's trained experts in reading signs and dreams. They had their methods and their books. They cannot read these dreams.

And now, at last, the cupbearer remembers. ‘Today I recall my failures.’ It has taken a crisis at court to jog his memory. Two years late, it is exactly the right moment.
passages.later: The same scene comes again in Babylon. King Nebuchadnezzar's wise men cannot explain his dream, and Daniel says there is “a God in heaven who reveals mysteries” (Daniel 2:28). Daniel and his friends were found “ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom” (Daniel 1:20).
passages.asks: Joseph waited two more years for a man to remember him, and God's timing turned out to be exact. Ask what you have been waiting for that seems forgotten. Then ask whether you can trust that God has not forgotten, even when people have.

passages.happening:
“So Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who was quickly brought out of the dungeon. After he had shaved and changed his clothes, he went in before Pharaoh” (verse 14).

Pharaoh says, “I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it” (verse 15).

“I myself cannot do it,” Joseph replies, “but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer” (verse 16).

Pharaoh tells his dreams again (verses 17-24). He adds, “I have never seen such ugly cows in all the land of Egypt!” (verse 19), and that after eating the fat cows the thin ones looked just as thin as before (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
In one morning Joseph goes from the dungeon to the throne room. He shaves and changes his clothes. Egyptian men of rank were usually clean-shaven, while Egyptian pictures often show men from Canaan with beards. Joseph is made fit to stand before the king.

Notice the clothes again. Joseph's life can be told by what he wore: the robe his brothers stripped off him, the cloak he left in the hand of Potiphar's wife, the prison clothes he now takes off. Soon he will wear fine linen.

Pharaoh praises Joseph's skill. Joseph's first words turn the praise away. ‘I myself cannot do it.’ In Hebrew it is one short word, meaning ‘apart from me’ or ‘not me’. After thirteen years of slavery and prison, here is his chance to impress the most powerful man in the world. He gives the credit to God.

Pharaoh's own retelling adds details. He is disgusted by the thin cows, and he is disturbed that they looked no better after eating. It is a picture of a famine so deep that even plenty cannot fill it.
passages.later:
A psalm tells this moment from God's side: “until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right. The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free” (Psalm 105:19-20).

Peter writes, “Humble yourselves, therefore, under God's mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6).
passages.asks: Joseph's first words to the most powerful man in the world were ‘Not me.’ Ask whether you take credit for gifts that God gave you. Then ask how you might point beyond yourself the next time someone praises you.

passages.t: Seven years of plenty, seven of famine
passages.happening:
“The dreams of Pharaoh are one and the same. God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do” (verse 25).

The seven good cows and seven good heads of grain are seven years of plenty. The seven thin ones are seven years of famine (verses 26-27). “Behold, seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the land of Egypt, but seven years of famine will follow them” (verses 29-30).

“Because the dream was given to Pharaoh in two versions, the matter has been decreed by God, and He will carry it out shortly” (verse 32).

Then Joseph gives advice. Pharaoh should find “a discerning and wise man” and set him over Egypt (verse 33). Officials should collect a fifth of the harvest in the good years (verse 34) and store the grain in the cities (verse 35). “This food will be a reserve for the land during the seven years of famine” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
Twice Joseph says it: God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do (verses 25, 28). Pharaoh was the most powerful man in that world. Here the God of a Hebrew slave tells Pharaoh what will happen in Pharaoh's own country.

A dream given twice means the matter is settled. Joseph's own dreams came in pairs (chapter 37). So did the officers' (chapter 40). Now Pharaoh's.

Then Joseph does more than explain. He makes a plan. Save in the good years for the bad. Take a fifth of the harvest and store it. He does not stop at telling Pharaoh what God will do. He tells him what a wise ruler should do about it.

Notice too what Joseph does not do. He does not ask for the job. He says Pharaoh should find a wise man. He does not put his own name forward.

Was there an Egyptian memory of seven lean years? A much later inscription carved on a rock on Sehel Island, near Aswan in the far south of Egypt, tells of a seven-year famine in the days of the ancient king Djoser. It was carved in the Ptolemaic period, the last centuries before Christ. Scholars now see the seven-year famine as a theme known across the ancient Near East. The inscription does not tell us about Joseph. It shows that the idea of seven lean years was at home in that world.
passages.later:
Proverbs praises the same foresight in a small creature: the ant “prepares its provisions in summer; it gathers its food at harvest” (Proverbs 6:8).

Stephen tells what came next: “Then famine and great suffering swept across Egypt and Canaan, and our fathers could not find food” (Acts 7:11).
passages.asks: Joseph trusted God's word and still made a careful plan. Ask whether you treat trusting God and planning ahead as opposites. Then ask what wise preparation, not worry, would look like in your home or work this year.

passages.happening:
Pharaoh asks his officials, “Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?” (verse 38). He tells Joseph, “You shall be in charge of my house” (verse 40). “I hereby place you over all the land of Egypt” (verse 41).

“Then Pharaoh removed the signet ring from his finger, put it on Joseph's finger, clothed him in garments of fine linen, and placed a gold chain around his neck” (verse 42). Joseph rides in Pharaoh's second chariot, and men call out before him, “Bow the knee!” (verse 43).

“Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah, and he gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife” (verse 45).

“Now Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt” (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
In one day the prisoner becomes second only to the king. ‘Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you’ (verse 40).

Pharaoh speaks of ‘the Spirit of God’. He probably meant a divine spirit as he understood it, among Egypt's many gods. The Hebrew could also be read ‘the spirit of the gods’. But the narrator lets his words say more than he knew.

Now look at what Joseph is given. A signet ring carried the king's seal. With it Joseph could sign orders in Pharaoh's name. Fine linen was the prized cloth of Egypt. A gold chain around the neck was a mark of high honor. And a chariot. The boy whose robe was torn off by his brothers is dressed by a king.

The cry “Bow the knee!” translates a rare word, abrek, that is probably Egyptian. Its exact meaning is uncertain.

Joseph is given an Egyptian name, Zaphenath-paneah. It is a real Egyptian kind of name, but scholars do not agree on what it means.

And he is given an Egyptian wife. Asenath is the daughter of Potiphera, a priest of On. On was the city the Greeks later called Heliopolis, ‘city of the sun’, near modern Cairo. It was a chief center of the worship of the sun god Ra. Many scholars think Asenath's own name means ‘she belongs to Neith’, an Egyptian goddess. Genesis states all of this plainly. It does not explain it or apologize for it.

Which Pharaoh was this? The text does not name him, and no Egyptian record names Joseph. The book page on Genesis notes that the patriarchs have traditionally been placed early in the second millennium BC, with Joseph's rise somewhat later, and that many scholars doubt the stories can be dated at all. Some readers link Joseph with the time of the Hyksos, rulers of West Asian origin, from Canaan and nearby lands, who held northern Egypt from about 1650 to 1550 BC; a man from Canaan, they say, could more easily rise under such kings. Others place him earlier, before the Hyksos. Others think the story was written much later and drew on knowledge of Egypt in its own day. These notes do not settle the question.
passages.later:
The psalm goes on: “He made him master of his household, ruler over all his substance” (Psalm 105:21).

Daniel's story has the same shape. After he explains the king's dream, “the king promoted Daniel and gave him many generous gifts” (Daniel 2:48). Mary sings of a God who “has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52).
passages.asks: Joseph was raised from a dungeon in a day, after thirteen years. Ask whether you believe God can change things suddenly after a long wait. Then ask how you would handle power if it came to you after years of being powerless.

passages.t: Plenty, two sons, and the famine
passages.happening:
In the seven good years the land grows plenty (verse 47). Joseph gathers the extra food and stores it in the cities, grain “like the sand of the sea” until no one can count it (verses 48-49).

“Before the years of famine arrived, two sons were born to Joseph by Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On” (verse 50). He names the first Manasseh: “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's household” (verse 51). He names the second Ephraim: “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction” (verse 52).

The seven years of famine begin, “just as Joseph had said” (verse 54). When the people cry to Pharaoh for food, he says, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you” (verse 55). Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain to the Egyptians (verse 56). “And every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain” (verse 57).
passages.hearers:
Grain like the sand of the sea. God promised Abraham descendants ‘like the sand on the seashore’ (22:17). The same picture is now used of food that will keep that family alive.

Joseph's two sons are born to an Egyptian mother, the daughter of a priest of On. Genesis says so plainly, twice (verses 45 and 50). These two boys will become two of the tribes of Israel. The people of God will include the grandsons of an Egyptian priest.

Listen to the names. Manasseh sounds like the Hebrew for ‘making forget’. Joseph says God has made him forget his hardship and his father's house. It is not that he has lost his memory; the pain no longer rules him. Yet the very name keeps the memory alive. Ephraim sounds like ‘fruitful’. ‘The land of my affliction’ is still what he calls Egypt. Even in his success, he does not pretend Egypt is home.

Then the famine comes, just as God showed. The storehouses open. The chapter ends with the whole world coming to Joseph for bread. God promised Abraham that ‘all the families of the earth’ would be blessed through his family (12:3). Here, in a small way, it begins.

This chapter tells only the start of Joseph's famine policy: a fifth of the harvest stored in the good years, and grain sold when the famine came. What happened in the later years of famine, and how it bore on the people of Egypt, comes in chapter 47, and the notes there face it.
passages.later:
On his deathbed Jacob takes Joseph's two sons as his own: “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine” (Genesis 48:5). He gives Israel a blessing in their names: “May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh” (Genesis 48:20).

Pharaoh's words, “do whatever he tells you”, are echoed by Mary at the wedding in Cana: “Do whatever He tells you” (John 2:5).
passages.asks: Joseph named one son for healing and the other for fruit in a hard land. Ask what God has helped you stop being ruled by. Then ask where he has made you fruitful in a place you never wanted to be.
